title: Resonant Frequency Reduction of Piezoelectric Voltage Energy Harvester by Elastic Boundary Condition

sections.heading: RESONANT FREQUENCY REDUCTION OF PIEZOELECTRIC VOLTAGE ENERGY HARVESTER BY ELASTIC BOUNDARY CONDITION

sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text:
Most vibration-based energy harvesters, including piezoelectric harvester system, perform efficiently at only its resonant frequency as linear resonators, usually at very high frequency which are out of the range of frequency of interest. In real life applications, these linear resonators are impractical since real ambient vibrations are simply having varying lower frequencies. Hence, design a tuneable vibration energy harvester at a lower and useful frequency range of interest are essential in allowing promising energy output to meet intended power input at a more practical approach. In this paper, the piezoelectric voltage energy harvester (PVEH) was designed with a flexible fixture with the aim to reduce its first fundamental natural frequency. Two thickness of elastic fixtures were applied to generate power on PVEH. Three experimental techniques were used to measure the vibration characteristics of PVEH. First, the full-field optical technique, amplitude-fluctuation electronic speckle pattern interferometry (AF-ESPI) measured simultaneously the resonant frequencies and mode shapes. This is followed by the pointwise measurement system, laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) in which the resonant frequencies were measured by dynamic signal swept-sine analysis. The resonant frequencies and anti-resonant frequencies were also obtained by impedance analysis. The results obtained from experimental measurements were compared with finite element numerical calculation. It is found that the boundary conditions under the elastic fixtures can effectively reduce the resonant frequency of the PVEH with a reasonable voltage output. The fundamental natural frequency of PVEH with the thickness of $0 . 5 8 – \mathrm { m m }$ elastic fixture is reduced to $3 7 \mathrm { H z }$ maintaining at 7.1 volts $( 1 . 2 \mathrm { m W } )$ , in comparison with the natural frequency on cantilevered PVEH at $7 8 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ that produces 7.7 volts $( 6 . 5 \mathrm { m W } )$ ).

Keywords: piezoelectric energy harvester, natural frequency reduction, boundary condition, mode shape.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Energy harvesting techniques have been studied since last few decades and the research in this area is increasing drastically. However, practical usage of such techniques in real life devices is still limited. The available sources of vibration energy include human body motion, vibration of structures like buildings and vehicles, and the continuous flow of fluid. To transform mechanical energy from ambient vibration into electrical energy, different types of energy harvesting techniques are available, including electromagnetic, electrostatic, magnetostriction, and piezoelectric.

Wei and Jing [1] illustrated the theory and modelling methods behind each of these techniques together with their own configuration designs and realization. Each of these techniques has its own specialties and thus only suitable for a certain specific application based on the case conditions to achieve maximum output. For example, piezoelectric materials are normally thin membranes and thus have an advantage of size in limited space. Piezoelectric energy harvesting is getting more attentions globally in recent years. Mutsuda, et al. [2] developed a highly flexible piezoelectric energy harvester in flowinduced vibration to convert ambient kinetic energy such as mechanical vibration, ocean and wind energy into electric power. He et al. [3] fabricated a self-charging power cell (SCPC) to convert and store the vibration mechanical energy of human motion using mesoporous PVDF-LiPF6 film as piezo-electrolyte. The high stability and storage capacity of this SCPC allow it to power various wearable electronics, including sports bracelet, smartwatch and LEDs. Piezoelectric transducer is considered as a good power generator due to its high power density and no external voltage source requirement [4]. The most popular type of setup for piezoelectric vibration energy harvester (PVEH) system is the bimorph rectangular cantilever beam configuration because of its sensitivity. Basically, the setup of system is fixed one end as cantilever plate allowing it for free movement, most frequently while mounted a mass on the plate at the same time. Many researchers improvised on this basic setup and come out with their novel designs to further increase the performance and efficiency of PVEH. Thein et al. [5] simulated the output power of their piezoelectric generator designs using finite element analysis (FEA) and then verified all the simulations, experimental and theoretical results. The authors then optimized the structure of cantilever beam, by which the power is maximized and structural volume is minimized simultaneously. Similarly, Xie et al. [6] designed a tapered shape cantilever to compare with the available uniform shape cantilever harvester in terms of maximum power output and energy harvesting efficiency. Allamraju and Srikanth [7], Lu et al. [8], and Tabesh and Fréchette [9] all used cantilever beam as their model of piezoelectric energy harvester with different sources of excitation force because the mathematical models were proposed in their designs of optimization. There is also a harvesting technique which discards the presence of proof mass and structural vibration for generation of power. It utilizes the flow of fluids, both liquid and air, to create a vortex region as the vibration source after passing through an obstructed splitter body. Chin et al. [10] made use of splitter body to build a low velocity, high pressure vortex region near the PVEH plate to excite the tip of plate. It was shown that the contribution of resultant vortex frequency matching with natural frequency is more important than fluctuating lift force in improving vibrational amplitude, even though both are affected by the wind speed. Similarly, Akaydin et al. [11] demonstrated that base excitation is not the only way for piezoelectric harvesting. They investigated the voltage generated by piezoelectric cantilever beam placed in turbulent boundary layers and wakes of circular cylinders at high Reynolds numbers. An interesting specification in their study is the implementation of threeway coupled interaction simulation that takes into account the aerodynamics, structural vibration, and electrical response of piezoelectric generator. Song et al. [12] designed a novel PVEH using macro fiber composite cantilever with a bi-cylinder in water to produce energy conversion by means of vortex-induced vibration (VIV)

and wake-induced vibration (WIV). With optimal resistance $( 1 7 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ and cylinder diameter $( 3 0 ~ \mathrm { m m } )$ , the maximum power output, $2 1 . 8 6 \mu \mathrm { W }$ is generated at a water velocity of $0 . 3 1 ~ \mathrm { m / s }$ .

In order to generate maximum voltage and displacement response, it is preferred for driving frequency to meet or to be near with the harvester’s natural frequency to induce the resonance phenomenon. Roundy et al. [4] stated that low level vibrations occurring in our environment appear to have a fundamental mode on the order of $1 0 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , and maximum acceleration magnitudes in the range of $0 . 5 - 5$ $\mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . Hence piezoelectric harvester with wide bandwidth is always preferred to cover all scale of peak frequency. Yuantai et al. [13] studied on bimorph cantilever to prove that applying axial preload to adjust the device frequency successfully raised the harvester power output. Recently, some researchers achieved on reducing the resonant frequency for several designs of PVEH, regardless of adding proof mass. By combing with arch-folk structure, Hu et al [14] proposed a novel frequency-tunable PVEH for reduced order modeling with improved power generation. The change on natural frequency on the proposed design was reported from $9 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ to $7 7 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ . Tian et al. [15] removed a rectangle hole on the central part of cantilever plate to reduce the natural frequency for PVEH. The study involved structural optimization and considered the loss in power density of the design. Yang et al [16] used flat and s-shape cantilever plate to design PVEH in reducing the first two natural modes. The 1st (2nd) natural frequency was only decreased from $4 4 \ \mathrm { H z }$ (50Hz) to 37 Hz $2 3 \ \mathrm { H z } )$ ). Toyabur et al [17] and Murotani et al [18] applied on electromagnetic coil and bi-stable electrostatic spring, respectively, to study on tunable multi-modal energy harvesting system. However, the re-dundant electric power usage was reported in this design and the shift of frequency was limited.

Another property of vibration worth considered is the mode shape of piezoelectric harvester, which would determine which part of the entire system possess highest response amplitude. Wu et al. [19] did a massive job on investigating the resonant frequencies and mode shapes of piezoelectric rectangular plate from theoretical analysis, numerical calculation and experimental measurement. Their results showed good agreement in comparison and reported that specific vibration modes are easily excited by manipulating the configuration of electrodes to enhance the excited efficiency of piezoelectric plate. At the same time, Yee et al. [20] used Experimental Modal Analysis (EMA) and Operating Deflection Shape (ODS) for optimal location selection scheme to improve the vibration energy harvesting process. Based on their results, voltage harvested can improve by $3 3 . 3 \%$ when piezoelectric plate is placed at high displacement antinodal points, conversely significant reduction $( > 7 0 \% )$ of voltage is detected at any minimum vibration nodal points.

Most vibration-based energy harvesters, including piezoelectric harvester system, perform efficiently at only its resonant frequency or within the respective limited bandwidth, as linear resonators, usually at very high frequency which are out of the range of frequency of interest. In real life applications, these linear resonators are impractical since real ambient vibrations are of random excitations spreading over wide frequency range or simply having varying lower frequencies. Hence, extending operational bandwidth of vibration energy harvester or design a tunable vibration energy harvester at a lower and useful frequency range of interest are essential in allowing promising energy output to meet intended power input at a more practical approach.

In this paper, the piezoelectric voltage energy harvester (PVEH) is designed with the aim to reduce its natural frequencies base on the boundary conditions change. This study presents the concept of feasibility in changing a cantilevered PVEH’s boundary through adding flexi-ble support to reduce the PVEH’s resonant frequency in order to improve the practicality of the PVEH in industrial applications. The different thickness of flexible fixture is clamped to the PZT. Finite element commercial software, ABAQUS (Dassault Systèmes Simulia Corp., Providence, RI) [21] is used to calculate on the resonant frequencies and under different boundary conditions. The vibration characteristics results are experimentally validated by variety of experimental methods to confirm its effect on frequency reduction.

sections.heading: 2.1 Designs of Elastic Boundary for PVEH
sections.text:
The elastic fixtures were designed under two thicknesses, i.e., $1 \mathrm { m m }$ and $0 . 5 8 \mathrm { m m }$ to study the effect of resonant frequency reduction. The elastic fixtures structure consists of three parts, i.e., aluminum cover, PZT and aluminum elastic support base. The schematic diagram of the elastic fixture of PVEH is shown in Figure 1 where the exposed length of the PZT is $5 8 ~ \mathrm { \ m m }$ Extended fixture is designed for reducing natural frequency, and the L-shape is convenient manufactured by electrical discharge machine (EDM). Hence, the $0 . 5 8 – \mathrm { m m }$ thickness is limited on the common fabrication in EDM.

In experimental measurements, only the end of fixture part was clamped by vise holder as shown in Figure 2. In the experiments of direct piezoelectric effect (DPE), the shaker was used to excite the end part of fixture. Conversely, the experiments of converse piezoelectric effect (CPE), the electric voltages input was used to excite piezoelectric plate to generate the vibration characteristics.

In order to compare the reduction of resonant frequency of the proposed elastic fixtures, the PVEH under the cantilevered boundary condition was used as benchmark for comparison. The end of piezoelectric plate was clamped on a structure and excited by DPE and CPE, respectively. The schematic diagram and experimental set-up of the PVEH under the cantilevered boundary condition which was clamped by vise holder are shown in Figures 3 and 4. In the experiment of DPE, the shaker was attached to the end base of PVEH.

sections.heading: 3. EXPERIMENTAL TECHNIQUES
sections.text:
In this study, three experimental techniques i.e. amplitude-fluctuation electronic speckle pattern interferometry (AF-ESPI), laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV), and impedance analysis were used to measure the vibration characteristics of the piezoelectric plate. An introduction of these experimental techniques is briefly provided in this section.

sections.heading: 3.1 Transversal vibration measurement by AF-ESPI
sections.text:
The schematic of optical AF-ESPI setup for measuring the transversal resonant frequencies and corresponding vibration mode shapes of piezoelectric plate is shown in Figure 5. The laser beam is divided into two paths by a beamsplitter. One is the object beam and the other is the reference beam. The object beam injects to the specimen and reflects to the charge-coupled device (CCD, Guppy PRO F-201, Allied Vision Technologies GmbH, Stadtroda, Germany). The reference beam reflected from a reference plate to the CCD camera through a beamsplitter. The interferogram is stored in an image recorded by the CCD camera as buffer as a first image, when the specimen is excited in vibration. Then the second image is grabbed and subtracted by the image processing system. Only randomly distributed speckles are shown in the monitor if the frequency deviates far from the resonant frequency. If the frequency is approaching to the resonant frequency, the finer fringe patterns are corresponding to the mode shape observed in monitor. The number of fringes are increase and clearer as the resonant frequency of excited specimen, and record by the computer. Hence, the resonant frequencies and the correspondent mode shapes can be determined simultaneously.

The principle of AF-ESPI is based on the following concept in vibration measurement. The interferogram of vibration is recorded by a CCD and is shown real-time on the monitor as the speckle fringe pattern, while the specimen vibrates at a specific frequency. Based on the time-averaging method, the light intensity of the image, $I ( x , y )$ , can be expressed as

$$
I = \frac { 1 } { \tau } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau } \left\{ { { I _ { o } } + I _ { R } } + 2 \sqrt { I _ { o } { I _ { R } } } \cos \atop { \left[ { \not { D } + \frac { 2 \pi } { \lambda } { A } ( 1 + \cos \theta ) \cos \omega t } \right] } \right\} } d t
$$

where $\tau$ is the CCD refresh time, $I _ { o }$ is the object light intensity, $I _ { \scriptscriptstyle R }$ is the reference light intensity, $\phi$ is the phase difference between the object and reference light, $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the laser, $A$ is the vibration amplitude, $\omega$ is the angular frequency, and $\theta$ is the angle between the object light and observation direction of specimen for the transverse vibration setup. It should be noted that $\phi$ and $A$ are functions of the position on the vibration surface. The derivation of Eqn. (1) in detail had been proposed by Wang et al [23] and Huang and Ma [24].

Based on the time-averaged method, assume the vibration period is much smaller than the CCD refresh time (i.e., $\tau > > 2 \pi / \omega$ ). The vibration measurement includes many periods of object motion during the camera frame period. From the transversal vibration setup, set the function of sensitivity as

$$
r = \frac { 2 \pi ( 1 + \cos \theta ) } { \lambda }
$$

Then, Eqn. (1) can be simplified as

$$
I _ { 1 } = I _ { O } + I _ { R } + 2 \sqrt { I _ { O } I _ { R } } ( \cos \phi ) J _ { 0 } ( \varGamma A )
$$

where $J _ { 0 }$ is a zero-order Bessel function of the first kind. The optic field in static term, $( I _ { O } + I _ { R } )$ , disturbs on the steady-state fringe pattern resolution. To eliminate this term from the first image is subtracted into a second vibrating image. The light intensity of the second image is represented as

$$
I _ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { \tau } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau } } { \left\{ { I _ { O } + I _ { R } + 2 \sqrt { I _ { O } I _ { R } } \cos { \omega t } } \atop { \left[ \phi + I ( A + A A ) \cos { \omega t } \right] } \right\} } d t
$$

Using the Taylor series expansion and neglecting the higher order terms, Eqn. (4) can be rewritten as

$$
I _ { 2 } = I _ { O } + I _ { R } + 2 \sqrt { I _ { O } I _ { R } } \biggl [ 1 { - } \frac { 1 } { 4 } \Gamma ^ { 2 } ( A A ) ^ { 2 } \biggr ] J _ { 0 } ( \Gamma A )
$$

The result represents that the fringes patterns of the transversal vibrations obtained by AF-ESPI are dominated by a zero-order Bessel function $J _ { 0 }$ from Eqn. (6). For $A = 0$ , i.e. the nodal line in vibration, the zero-order Bessel function has the maximum value. It is also shown

$$
I = \big | I _ { 2 } - I _ { 1 } \big | = \frac { \sqrt { I _ { O } I _ { R } } } { 2 } \big | ( \cos \phi ) \varGamma ^ { 2 } ( A A ) ^ { 2 } J _ { 0 } ( \varGamma A ) \big |
$$

The other vibrating amplitude, $A _ { i }$ , for the ith dark fringe in AF-ESPI experimental measurement can be quantitatively determined from the roots of $J _ { 0 } ( \Gamma A ) = 0$ . In the selfarranged AF-ESPI setup, the light source uses on the He-Ne laser with a wavelength of $\lambda = 6 3 2 . 8$ nm. Hence, the vibration amplitudes for the first seven bright fringes are $A _ { i }$ $( \mathrm { i } = 1 { \sim } 7 ) = 0$ , 0.192, 0.354, 0.512, 0.752, 0.910 and $1 . 0 6 8 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ . Hence, the vibration amplitudes of mode shapes obtained from the AF-ESPI experimental setup are on the resolution of sub-micrometer order.

sections.heading: 3.2 Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDV)
sections.text:
The LDV system (Model: PDV-100, Polytec GmbH Waldbronn, German) [25] provides a point-wise velocity measurement, which is perpendicular to the surface, with ultra-high resolution (on the 5, 25, and $1 2 5 \mathrm { m m / s }$ per volts) and has a wide signal bandwidth ( $0 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ to $2 2 \mathrm { k H z }$ ). The non-contact optical system is based on the principles of a Michelson interferometer and the Doppler effect. With this type of interferometer, a high-frequency carrier signal is generated on the photo detector with an acoustic optical modulator (Bragg cell). To achieve the vibration measurement, the beam of a helium neon laser is injected on the vibrating object and scattered back from it. Although the original data from LDV is measured on the velocity, the excited source is based on the steady-state signal to calculate easily as the displacement (to divide by $2 \pi \mathrm { f } )$ or acceleration (to multiply by $2 \pi f$ ). In the present study, the excited input was from the piezoelectric specimen in the measurements of converse piezoelectric effect, and the mechanical shaker (Model: V4, Data physics corporation, UK) was used in the measurements of direct piezoelectric effect and voltage output. The swept-sine signal generated by function generator (Model number: 33210A, Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA), was controlled by MATLAB software in personal computer in which the steady-state excitation was applied to vibrate the PVEH. When the PVEH was stimulated by piezoelectric converse effect or shaker as shown in Figure 6, the velocity measured by LDV system was sent to oscilloscope (Model number: DSOX2004A, Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) and was recorded by computer. Hence, the frequency response can be obtained in which the peaks presented as local maxima in the response curve are the resonant frequencies for transversal vibration. Although the LDV system can measure precisely the wide-range vibrational displacements over several seconds at very high frequency, however, it is more time-consuming for swept-sine excitation in obtaining full-field vibrational displacements from point by point measurement.

sections.heading: 3.3 Impedance Analysis
sections.text:
Electric impedance is an important parameter when piezoelectric materials are uses on the components of mechatronics. The resonant frequency and anti-resonant frequencies, of piezoelectric elements, $f _ { r }$ and $f _ { a }$ , respectively, are measured through impedance analysis and the electromechanical coupling coefficient is represented as $$ k _ { d } = \sqrt { \frac { f _ { a } ^ { 2 } - f _ { r } ^ { 2 } } { f _ { a } ^ { 2 } } } $$ The impedance response curves of PVEH were obtained using an impedance analyzer (E4990A, Keysight Technologies) shown in Figure 7 ranging from $2 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ to $7 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . The resonant frequencies can be obtained by response curve of impedance analysis from the local minima, and the anti-resonant frequencies are obtained from the resonance curve of local maxima. Zhou et al. [26] have proposed to an electromechanical model related to impedance and velocity to demonstrate the vibration characteristics of piezoelectric components. sections.heading: 4.1 Vibration Characteristics of PVEH under cantilevered boundary condition
sections.text:

It is noted that the resonant frequencies as well as the corresponding mode shapes obtained by ESPI are close to the simulation results from ABAQUS. It can be observed that the torsional modes is excited by DPE and this is consistent with the past research results as discussed in [22] and [28]-[30]. There is no torsional mode excited by CPE. respectively. It is found that the results of impedance analysis are close to the results measured by LDV and ESPI. Figure 11 shows the measurement results of LDV under swept-sine signal from $0 { - } 7 0 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ by DPE. It is also observed that the first three modes of PVEH are obtained the frequencies measured by LDV are close to the results of simulation. The relationship between the frequency and the output voltage under DPE is shown in Figure 12. It is noted that the peak values of the output voltage of PZT are located at bending modes of the first and the third resonant frequencies. The output voltage of PZT is recorded at 7.8V under the first resonant frequency at $8 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . It is worthwhile to mention that the focus of the present study is mainly on the piezoelectric components in which the electromechanical coupling efficiency is concerned. The largest bending deformation of the PZT will subsequently give larger output voltage.. From the mode shapes obtained by ESPI as shown in Figure 8, the corresponding first 2 bending modes are $8 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ and $4 7 4 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , respectively in which the maximum output voltage is observed at the first bending mode as shown in Figure 12. On the other hand, there is only small voltage output recorded at torsional mode of $2 9 8 \mathrm { H z }$ due to the excitation point of the shaker is located at the nodal point of the torsional mode giving minimum response and output voltage. There are also redundant peaks observed at $2 5 \mathrm { H z }$ in Figures 11, and at $4 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ and $1 3 4 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ in Figure 12, respectively. These additional peaks were mainly the rigid body modes of the PZT and aluminum fixture when it was direct contacted and excited by the shaker. The PZT and fixture undergoes relatively higher rigid body deformation in which the PZT itself has small bending deformation. Thus, these frequency components give relatively lower output voltage.

sections.heading: 4.2.1 The 1-mm elastic fixture
sections.text:
Figure 13 shows the comparison of natural frequencies and their corresponding mode shapes obtained between ABAQUS simulation and the ESPI measurement under CPE and DPE. It is found that the resonant frequencies of ESPI and simulation are close, and the mode shapes show high similarity of correlation. As observed in cantilevered condition, the torsional modes, i.e., second mode, fifth mode and seventh mode are not excited under CPE. It is also noted that there are three types of vibration characteristics where the first is the elastic fixture vibration, the second is PZT vibration and the third is the vibration from elastic fixture and PZT combined. The first and second modes obtained are the first type of vibration characteristics, i.e. the elastic fixture vibration where PZT is driven by the elastic support. The third, fifth and sixth modes are classified as the second type of vibration characteristics. From the figure, it is observed that the elastic fixture is stationary while the PZT dominates the deformation. The fourth and eighth modes are classified as the third type where elastic fixture as well as the PZT deforms together. In addition, the torsional mode, i.e. fifth mode is excited under DPE. But the second and seventh modes of torsional modes are not excited. The main reason may be that the resonant frequencies of the two torsional modes are too close to the resonant frequency of the near bending modes. The PZT undergoes larger bending amplitude even at the resonant frequency of the torsion mode. The effect of torsion is relatively less significant due to the arrangement of the shaker excitation point and the torsional mode shapes and this explains the mode shapes of torsional mode cannot be measured. Figure 14 shows the measurement results of LDV under electrical excitation by CPE for elastic boundary condition using 1mm fixture. The frequencies measured by LDV are close to simulation, and the maximum vibration displacement is recorded at $6 3 \ \mathrm { H z }$ which is the first bending mode of PZT, i.e. third mode. Impedance analysis (Figure 15) also gives resonant frequencies which are close to the results measured by LDV and ESPI. Meanwhile, Figure 16 shows the measurement results of LDV under swept-sine signal from $0 { - } 7 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ by DPE. It is noted that the frequencies measured by LDV are similar with simulation. The measurement point has the largest vibration displacement at $2 3 \ \mathrm { ~ H z ~ }$ resonant frequency mainly due to the large rigid body deformation of the elastic fixture itself. Figure 17 shows the relationship between the frequency and the output voltage under DPE. The PZT gives the highest output voltage of $7 . 8 \mathrm { V p p }$ at the resonant frequencies of first bending modes at $6 6 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ and the output voltage is very small at the resonant frequencies of the torsional modes. This is consistent with the results of previous research [30] and it was explained in the preceding section. Although maximum displacement is recorded at $2 3 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , the output voltage at this frequency region is relatively smaller than the PZT first bending mode at $6 6 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . This is because at $2 3 \ \mathrm { ~ H z }$ , it is mainly dominated by the elastic fixture vibration, i.e. type one vibration characteristic where the PZT undergoes relatively lesser bending deformation and the large deformation at $2 3 \ \mathrm { H z }$ is mainly contributed by the rigid body deformation of the elastic fixture and subsequently gives larger deformation on the measured point at PZT. sections.heading: 4.2.3 Summary
sections.text: The voltage outputs shown in Figures 12, 17 and 22 under different boundary conditions are greatly affected by the resonance modes of the piezoelectric itself. The number of peaks observed in different boundary conditions represent the distinct dynamic behavior of the PVEH and its corresponding fixture. Every system under different geometrical properties, materials properties and boundary conditions have its own set of dynamic characteristics and number of peaks. Each peak represents the inherent behavior of the system at the specific frequency. In the present study, the number of peaks observed in voltage output correlated well with the experimental and computational results in ESPI, LDV, Impedance and FEM indicate the voltage output results obtained are reliable. On the other hand, the magnitude of peaks of in voltage output are different because of several factors. The study only focused on the PZT in which the direction and position of the shaker excitation is more sensitive to the bending modes of the PVEH itself, and thus, the bending modes are excited giving higher peak in voltage output compared with twisting modes. In addition, larger displacement as observed in the elastic fixture modes (Figure 11, 16, 21) is mainly contributed by the rigid body motion of the elastic fixture and PZT giving large deformation at the measurement point of PZT with small bending deformation. sections.heading: 4.3 Vibration Characteristics of PVEH under optimal elastic boundary condition
sections.text: The use of the $1 { \mathrm { - m m } }$ and $0 . 5 8 – \mathrm { m m }$ elastic fixture as discussed in preceding sections because both designs have the similar size (available space). However, the study is extended to the different round angles and thick-nesses by FEM to compare the results of the first two resonant frequencies without changing length based on the same material. The length of fixture in Figure 1 are fixed as $1 3 7 . 4 1 6 \mathrm { - m m }$ in length (the main part $1 0 0 \mathrm { - m m }$ length, $3 1 . 4 1 6 \mathrm { - m m } 9 0 ^ { \mathrm { o } }$ -arc length, and $6 { \cdot } \mathrm { m m }$ mounted part). The parameters of thickness (solid line in blue color) and round angles (dash line in red color) for elastic fixtures are gradually change and the first two natural modes, are determined using FEM. The geometric parameters for thickness are $1 . 2 8 \mathrm { m m }$ , $1 . 1 4 \mathrm { m m }$ , $1 . 0 0 \mathrm { m m }$ , $0 . 8 6 \mathrm { m m }$ , 0.72 mm, and $0 . 5 8 \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. The round angle are varied from $3 0 ^ { \mathrm { o } }$ , $6 0 ^ { \circ }$ , $9 0 ^ { \mathrm { o } }$ , $1 2 0 ^ { \circ }$ , $1 5 0 ^ { \mathrm { o } }$ , and $1 8 0 ^ { \mathrm { o } }$ , respectively with the thickness is kept to $1 { \mathrm { - m m } }$ thickness. It is noted that both the 1st or 2nd resonant bending modes for the PVEH are affected by the boundary changes. The reduction in natural frequency is obvious when the round angle of the elastic fixture used exceeds $3 0 ^ { \mathrm { o } }$ . The largest reduction in natural frequency is observed on round angle of $1 8 0 ^ { \circ }$ . On the other hand, the thinner elastic fixture in thickness shows the greater reduction in natural frequency in which $0 . 5 8 \mathrm { m m }$ shows the greatest reduction. It is concluded that using larger round angle and thinner elastic fixture can effectively reduce the natural frequencies for PVEH.

sections.heading: 5. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text: The elastic fixtures designed used in this study can effectively reduce the resonant frequency of PVEH. The first (second) natural frequency 78Hz (485Hz) of PVEH under cantilevered boundary condition is reduced to $6 3 \mathrm { H z }$ $( 1 4 7 \mathrm { H z } )$ and $3 7 \mathrm { H z }$ (197Hz) for PVEH respectively with the $1 { \mathrm { - m m } }$ and $0 . 5 8 – \mathrm { m m }$ thickness of elastic fixture. The vibration characteristics obtained by FEM showed excellent agreement with the results obtained by three experimental measurements. At the corresponding 1st vibration mode, the voltage outputs were recorded at 7.7 volts $( 6 . 5 \mathrm { m W } )$ ), 7.9 volts $( 5 . 1 \mathrm { m W } )$ and 7.1 volts $( 1 . 2 \mathrm { m W } )$ , respectively for cantilever, $1 { \mathrm { - m m } }$ thickness elastic fixture, and $0 . 5 8 – \mathrm { m m }$ thickness elastic fixture boundary conditions. The PVEH is able to harvest promising energy output at a lower and useful frequency range of interest at a more practical approach.
